title: How to get this to work? Dockerfile FROM {YourPrivateRepo.azurecr.io/some/repo}
author: Kbdavis07

posts.author: Kbdavis07
posts.text:
FROM microsoft/aspnet

Would like to use instead

FROM MyPrivateRepo.azurecr.io/some/repo

If this is possible how do I pass my login info?

I am very new to using Docker and Dockerfile and could not find anything on the net on how to use your own Private registry instead of Docker Hub.

I am trying to use the Azure Container registry to build my container with.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-get-started-docker-cli

Since Docker Hub you can only have 1 free private repo at a time without having to upgrade and pay for it.

Currently testing out the Private Azure Container registry and works great, can push and pull my images into and out of it with no issues.

Just had not figured out how to do that in a Dockerfile or some automated task in Visual Studio Team Services.

Trying to also figure out away to reduce the amount of time it takes to build on Visual Studio Team services currently taking about 9 mins just to download the base image microsoft/aspnet.

I have a VM set up in Azure that has docker installed, is there a method to build from there remotely in Visual Studio Team services as it is already cache there and only takes a few mins to build from there locally.

Any help would be great.

posts.author: Siva G
posts.text:
I tried these two scenarios and both of them works:

- Local machine

- On my Linux machine, run 'docker login myregistry.azurecr.io'

- Author Dockerfile with 'FROM: myregistry.azurecr.io/image1'

- docker build .
This worked fine.

- Visual Studio Online build

- Used docker extension https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-vscs-rm.docke‌​r , to build the same dockerfile in 1.

- Configured "Build and Image" task, with myregistry.azurecr.io

- Schedule the build on 'Hosted Linux Preview' Agent
It worked great. I can see in the console log that the task first executes docker login myregistry.azurecr.io and then runs the 'docker build' command.

posts.author: Sebastian
posts.text:
You need to perform a login first.

docker login MyPrivateRepo.azurecr.io

This stores the encoded credentials in $HOME/.docker/config.json and you can build Dockerfiles which contain references to your private repository.

posts.text:
-
As the column address is a String type (dictionary as string), it might not have been unpacked as the rest.

-
In order to unpack this column, you can use json_tuple() provided by pyspark.sql.functions. Look at the following code.

-
I have taken a sample dataframe only with the values of address. The following is the schema of that dataframe.

root
 |-- id: long (nullable = true)
 |-- address: string (nullable = true)

#id column only for demonstration.

- Now you can use json_tuple() to create seperate columns for each of the key inside address object.

d2 = df.select(col("id"),json_tuple(col("address"),"address_components","formatted_address","geometry","place_id","types")) \
    .toDF("id","address_components","formatted_address","geometry","place_id","types")
d2.printSchema()

#schema is
root
 |-- id: long (nullable = true)
 |-- address_components: string (nullable = true)
 |-- formatted_address: string (nullable = true)
 |-- geometry: string (nullable = true)
 |-- place_id: string (nullable = true)
 |-- types: string (nullable = true)

- If you want to further parse each of the row, you can use many necessary functions provided by pyspark.sql.functions to transform data as required.

title: How to organize signing process of docker images in CI pipe?
author: Kirill Rudnev

posts.author: Kirill Rudnev
posts.text:
Good afternoon.

We have a container image development and assembly infrastructure built on Gitlab. The developer develops the code and commits it to GitLab. The container image is assembled using GitLab-runner mechanisms. We are using the free version of Gitlab, and we do not have the option to use the commercial version. For this reason, we cannot use multiple "approves" for the same code.

- Before assembling the container image, SCA, code review, and SAST are checked.

- After the container image is built, it is uploaded to the image storage of the development environment (local Docker hub DEV).

- After the container image is assembled, the container is launched in a test environment and DAST testing is performed.

- After testing, the image is copied to the storage of the product environment (local Docker hub PROD).

The question is : we want to ensure that at each of the steps of passing the container image through the pipe, a process of approving works for its further passage. For example, a code review occurs first. The team makes a code review and puts an "approve", after which the image goes for further checks. Further, similarly with SCA, SAST, DUST, etc.  If the tests are automatic, then according to the successful results of passing the automatic test, the "approve" should be set automatically. After passing all the tests, a runner should be called, which will check that all the necessary applications have been received and run the "cosign" utility to sign the container and upload the container to the storage of the product environment (local Docker hub PROD).

Please tell me how we could be organize such a process?

Thank you.

I tried to offer using comments in GitLab for approving, but team took this as bad idea.

posts.author: Alebs
posts.text:
What about :

- using separate CI pipelines for the steps and benefitting from the Gitlab's downstream pipelines.

- setting up manual validation for specific jobs, so that the pipeline will block until a manual "click on a button" is performed by a developer.

- using custom Gitlab variables ($SHOULD_THE_NEXT_STEP_RUN or $IS_SOME_TEST_OK = True / False), that would be set in one job and checked against in the following jobs.
